content:
Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the Department of Justice's request to reconsider his ruling allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 government agencies in its antitrust case. Here are the details.

A little background

One of Apple's defense strategies in the DOJ's antitrust lawsuit against Apple involves the U.S. government's own use of its products.

Apple's basic argument is that some of the practices the DOJ is challenging are actually legitimate security and privacy safeguards. To support this defense, Apple wants to know how federal agencies evaluate security and privacy when making smartphone policy and procurement decisions.

To do so, Apple has been trying to obtain documents from these 14 agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

After Apple initially moved to compel these agencies to produce documents, the DOJ objected. The dispute was then referred to Special Master Jose Linares for a ruling.

Last month, Linares granted Apple's request, prompting the DOJ to file a motion for reconsideration. The DOJ argued he used the wrong legal standard, that Apple's requests were overly burdensome and disproportionate, and that the documents sought were of only limited relevance to the case.

Apple then filed an opposition, arguing the DOJ's motion "does not hold up at any level" and rebutting the DOJ's arguments point by point.

Linares has now issued a new ruling, concluding that "none of the arguments raised by the DOJ in support of its motion for reconsideration are persuasive," and standing by his original decision.

Apple allowed to seek documents

The new ruling states:

The ruling added that Linares believed "there is no reason to change course at this time, with or without persuasive reasons," and noted that "in this case, the federal agencies are part of the United States for purposes of party discovery."

The ruling reads:

Plaintiffs attempt to nitpick, asserting that under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45, "non-parties to litigation receive greater protection in discovery than parties." [...] Plaintiffs therefore conclude that the Special Master's order and opinion were based on defective reasoning because they did not cite or incorporate Rule 45 as part of the analysis. The Special Master is familiar with Rule 45 and the different standards applicable to third-party discovery. A cursory review of the Special Master's opinion and order reveals that Plaintiffs' claim is simply wrong. Indeed, the Special Master detailed at length how this dispute arose. [...]. A review of that portion of the opinion and order reveals that it is the Plaintiffs who caused the subpoenas to be issued to the Defendants in the first place.

The document goes on to explain that Linares considers these 14 federal agencies to be part of the United States, rather than third parties entitled to additional protections under Rule 45:

The document also says the DOJ "misunderstands the legal framework applicable to this dispute," while criticizing the DOJ's claim that the requested information was of only "minimal" relevance as made "without citing any supporting evidence."

As a result, Apple is once again allowed to seek documents from the 14 federal agencies.
